title: Demonstration of Logical Error Suppression in a Surface Code Memory on a Cloud-Accessible IBM Superconducting Processor
authors: Shuwen Kan, Aaron Hoyt, Sean Garner, Ethan Vo, Adrian Harkness, Rod Rofougaran, Zefan Du, Chenxu Liu, Norm Tubman, Ying Mao, Samuel Stein
abstract: Quantum error correction can suppress logical errors exponentially with code distance when physical noise is below threshold. Realizing this on hardware requires tight coordination among quantum gates, mid-circuit measurements, and qubit coherence. Device variation, noise asymmetry, and correlations across space and time complicate the translation of these capabilities into logical error suppression. Here, we study rotated surface-code memory on an IBM Nighthawk r2 processor. Performance varies across tested processor placements, which we attribute to differences in qubit quality. We optimize the code by combining short readout, fused measurement and reset, and an XX echo on data qubits during ancilla readout. Compared with standard readout without reset or echo, the optimized syndrome extraction circuit reduces the median per-round logical error rate by factors of 3.8 in the X basis and 1.4 in the Z basis. In memory experiments of up to 150 rounds, the distance advantage weakens, alongside long-lived correlations that may reflect a persistent error component. Under our optimization recipe, increasing the protected distance from 3 to 6 while holding the other distance fixed reduces the per-round logical error rate from 0.53% to 0.24% in Z memory and from 0.52% to 0.22% in X memory. The corresponding error-suppression factors under maximum-likelihood decoding are 1.68 and 1.85. These results connect circuit compilation and optimization to surface-code memory performance and limitations, and motivate QPU and QEC circuit codesign for fault-tolerant quantum computing primitives on current cloud hardware.
summary: This work reports on achieving logical error suppression in a surface code memory on a superconducting quantum processor by optimizing the syndrome extraction circuit. Key optimizations, such as using fused measurement and reset, substantially lowered the logical error rate. The results highlight the critical interplay between circuit compilation, hardware noise characteristics, and the achievable performance of fault-tolerant quantum computation.
main_problem: The paper demonstrates the feasibility of achieving logical error suppression in a surface code memory using a cloud-accessible superconducting quantum processor.
main_result: Optimizing the syndrome extraction circuit significantly reduced the per-round logical error rate by factors up to 3.8 in the X basis, and increasing the protected distance from 3 to 6 further reduced the error rate.
method: The authors implemented and optimized syndrome extraction circuits, comparing performance across different readout and reset protocols.
model_or_system: The experiment uses a rotated surface-code memory implemented on an IBM Nighthawk r2 superconducting processor, which supports mid-circuit measurements and resets.
key_observables: Logical error probability (LEP), logical error per round ($\epsilon$), and error-suppression factors ($\Lambda$).
important_parameters: Protected distance (d=3 to d=6), readout duration, and echo pulse length.
main_assumptions: The analysis suggests that long-lived correlations and the weakening distance advantage point to persistent, non-Markovian error components in the hardware.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate processor layouts, performance comparisons of LEP vs. rounds, the effect of increasing protected distance, and the impact of echo pulses on flip probabilities.
paper_structure: The paper systematically analyzes performance by optimizing readout circuits (fused reset vs. standard), quantifying error suppression gains, and investigating the impact of idle time placement and echo pulses on coherence.
why_interesting: The detailed characterization of hardware limitations, such as data-qubit idling noise and the necessity of circuit-level optimization (e.g., fused reset, echo), provides crucial, actionable feedback for designing fault-tolerant quantum computation primitives.
